premium.faq.q.freeChange.message: Will the free version be cut back?

premium.faq.a.freeChange.message: No. The free version stays complete and will keep evolving at the same pace. Premium is for servers that need more: extended limits, advanced customization and early access.

premium.faq.q.lifetime.message: What does “price locked for life” mean?

premium.faq.a.lifetime.message: The Founder offer locks your price permanently. As long as your subscription stays active, your price never changes, even once new plans are introduced and the Founder offer is removed from the store.

premium.faq.a.activate.message: Type /settings on your Discord server and click “Premium”, or go straight to the RaidProtect store in Discord. Activation takes a few seconds.

premium.faq.a.cancel.message: Yes. The subscription is managed from Discord and can be cancelled whenever you want, with no commitment.

premium.faq.q.businessDiff.message: What's the difference between Founder and Business?

premium.faq.a.businessDiff.message: Founder unlocks bot customization and extended limits on every module. Business adds a dedicated, isolated instance plus human support (audit, custom integration, expert follow-up), on request.

mockup.settingsMenus.antispam.desc.message: Set up anti-spam to protect your Discord server from malicious user actions.

mockup.settingsMenus.antispam.high.message: 🔴 **High:** Sanctions all spam, including in ignored channels.

mockup.settingsMenus.antispam.medium.message: 🟡 **Medium:** Sanctions spam, but respects ignored channels.

mockup.settingsMenus.antispam.low.message: 🟢 **Low:** Only targets link, mention and selfbot spam.

mockup.settingsMenus.antispamSanctions.d.message: You can customize the sanctions applied depending on the type of spam detected. This allows for a response adapted to the severity of the violation.

mockup.settingsMenus.antispamSanctions.m.message: Replaces the trigger's sanction when spam spans several channels, only if it is more severe.

mockup.settingsMenus.antispamSanctions.p.message: Posts a message in the channel to announce the sanction (e.g. 'member has been muted'). Can be disabled with premium.

mockup.settingsMenus.reports.channelDesc.message: Configure the **channel** where **report notifications** will be sent.

mockup.settingsMenus.reports.roleDesc.message: Configure the **role that will be notified** when a **new report** is received. Typically, a moderator role.

mockup.settingsMenus.reports.notifyDesc.message: Choose **what reporters receive in DM** once their report has been handled.

mockup.settingsMenus.reports.trustedDesc.message: Members with this **trusted role** can apply a **preventive 24h timeout** when they report, pending moderator review.

mockup.settingsMenus.reports.badDesc.message: Act on members whose reports keep getting refused. Set the refused-report threshold, the time window, and what happens once the threshold is reached.

mockup.settingsMenus.reports.desc.message: Enable the **Reporting System** to allow members to **easily notify your team** of problematic situations.

mockup.settingsMenus.reports.groupValue.message: Reports about the same member are grouped into a single alert.

mockup.settingsMenus.reports.groupSepara.message: Every report creates its own separate alert.

mockup.settingsMenus.raidmode.thresholdD.message: Sets the maximum number of new members allowed to join the server within 10 seconds before RaidMode is activated.

mockup.settingsMenus.raidmode.durationDe.message: Sets the duration for which RaidMode remains active before automatically deactivating.

mockup.settingsMenus.raidmode.desc.message: Configure automatic anti-raid mode, which determines the maximum number of members that can join your server in 10 seconds. When the threshold is exceeded, flagged members are kicked and invites are disabled for the configured duration.

mockup.settingsMenus.raidmode.kickModeEn.message: Kicks members on join and sends them a DM with an invite to rejoin the server

mockup.settingsMenus.captcha.desc.message: Configure Captcha to prevent selfbots from accessing your Discord server and block raids.

mockup.settingsMenus.dmlock.desc1.message: Configure direct messages closing to prevent phishing or scam attempts.

mockup.settingsMenus.dmlock.desc2.message: RaidProtect will permanently disable direct messages until you disable this protection. We use the "Discord Security Actions" feature (limited to 24h by Discord, extended to always by RaidProtect).

mockup.settingsMenus.dmlock.warning.message: Only bots, members who have already exchanged or are friends and staff will be able to receive DMs with this mode.

mockup.settingsMenus.language.desc.message: The configured language only affects public messages sent by RaidProtect in your server (logs, captcha messages, reports, etc.). Private or temporary messages remain displayed in the language of the user interacting with the bot.

mockup.settingsMenus.prefix.desc1.message: Select a prefix for message commands. If none is set, message commands will be disabled.

mockup.settingsMenus.prefix.deleteDesc.message: **Delinvoke:** Automatically deletes the message containing the command when using prefix commands.

mockup.settingsMenus.logs.desc.message: By default, moderation logs are sent in the RaidProtect log channel. If you wish, you can select another channel.

mockup.settings.desc1.message: This menu allows you to view, adjust or customize features!

mockup.settings.desc2.message: Each category presents a list of customizable options in the form of buttons or dropdown menus. Use the buttons below to configure the various features and settings.

mockup.tagrole.desc3.message: Members will receive the role the next time they update their profile (Username, Avatar, Banner, Roles, Tag…). You can ask support for a full sync of the role if you have many members who currently have or previously had the tag.

learn.discord-nuke.metaTitle.message: Discord Nuke: What It Is and How to Protect Your Server
learn.discord-nuke.metaTitle.description: Learn article meta title: Discord nuke

learn.discord-nuke.metaDescription.message: A Discord nuke is the destruction of a server from the inside through permission abuse: deleted channels, mass bans. Definition, how it differs from a raid, and prevention.
learn.discord-nuke.metaDescription.description: Learn article meta description: Discord nuke

learn.discord-nuke.definition.message: A Discord nuke is the destruction of a server from the inside, by a member or bot holding elevated permissions: mass deletion of channels and roles, chain bans, spam via webhooks.

learn.discord-nuke.s1.p1.message: Unlike a raid, a nuke doesn't come from a wave of outside accounts: it starts from an account already on the server that holds elevated privileges.

learn.discord-nuke.s1.p2.message: Three cases come up most often: a staff member whose account is compromised ({token}, phishing), a malicious bot added with too many permissions, or a rogue moderator.

learn.discord-nuke.s1.p3.message: In a few seconds, a script deletes the channels, recreates hundreds of them to spam, bans members, and wipes the roles. That speed is what makes a nuke so destructive.

learn.discord-nuke.s2.h.message: Nuke or raid: what's the difference?

learn.discord-nuke.s2.intro.message: People often confuse the two, but the angle of attack is opposite, and so is the protection.

learn.discord-nuke.s2.summary.message: The takeaway: you don't protect against a nuke the way you protect against a {link}. Blocking arrivals is pointless if the threat already holds the keys to the server.

learn.discord-nuke.s3.i1.message: It's almost instant and often irreversible: deleted channels, messages, and roles can't be recovered natively.

learn.discord-nuke.s3.i2.message: Once it starts, it's hard to stop, because the attacker already has the permissions they need.

learn.discord-nuke.s3.i3.message: Banned members and a scattered community take a long time to rebuild, even after a restore.

learn.discord-nuke.s4.h.message: How to protect your server from a nuke?

learn.discord-nuke.s4.intro.message: The best defense happens upstream: a nuke almost always comes from a privileged account, so everything hinges on the trust you extend before handing out permissions.

learn.discord-nuke.s4.i1.b2.message: This is by far the most effective protection. Only grant "Administrator", "Manage Channels", or "Manage Roles" to people you genuinely trust, and give everyone the strict minimum: that's the principle of {link}.

learn.discord-nuke.s4.i2.b.message: Enable required two-factor authentication for moderation: a hacked staff account becomes much harder to exploit.

learn.discord-nuke.s4.i3.b.message: Only add trusted bots and remove admin from those that don't need it: a single compromised bot can nuke on its own.

learn.discord-nuke.s4.i4b.b.message: RaidProtect's {link} protects access to sensitive roles with an identity check (passkey, PIN, OTP) and temporary sessions: even a trusted person's account, if hacked, doesn't keep permanent admin access.

learn.discord-nuke.s4.i5.b.message: RaidProtect's {link} reviews your server's permissions and risky settings, and shows you what to fix.

learn.discord-nuke.faq.q1.message: Are a nuke and a raid the same thing?

learn.discord-nuke.faq.a1.message: No. A raid comes from the outside (a wave of accounts pouring in), while a nuke comes from the inside (an account or bot with permissions that destroys the server).

learn.discord-nuke.faq.q2.message: Can you recover a server after a nuke?

learn.discord-nuke.faq.a2.message: Deleted channels, messages, and roles can't be recovered natively: hence the importance of prevention. Bans, on the other hand, can be lifted as long as the server still exists.

learn.discord-nuke.faq.q3.message: Can a bot nuke my server?

learn.discord-nuke.faq.a3.message: Yes, if it holds elevated permissions. Only grant admin to trusted bots, and check the permissions of every bot you add.

learn.discord-nuke.faq.q4.message: Where does a compromised staff account come from?

learn.discord-nuke.faq.a4.message: Most often from a token stolen by a token grabber or a phishing attempt. That's why 2FA and caution around files and links are essential.

learn.discord-raid.metaTitle.message: Discord Raid: Definition and How to Protect Against It
learn.discord-raid.metaTitle.description: Learn article meta title: Discord raid

learn.discord-raid.metaDescription.message: A Discord raid is the coordinated arrival of dozens of accounts to spam and flood a server. Definition, how it differs from a nuke, and how to block it.
learn.discord-raid.metaDescription.description: Learn article meta description: Discord raid

learn.discord-raid.definition.message: A Discord raid is the sudden, coordinated arrival of many accounts, often bots, on a server, aiming to spam it, disrupt it, or flood it within minutes.

learn.discord-raid.s1.p1.message: A raid almost always follows the same script. An invite link leaks or is shared publicly, then a wave of accounts joins the server all at once.

learn.discord-raid.s1.p2.message: Once inside, the participants go on the attack: mass messages, repeated {code} mentions, scam links, shocking images, or emoji floods. The goal is to {strong}.

learn.discord-raid.s1.p3.message: Most raids are automated: not humans but bots driven from a single tool, capable of going from a few accounts to several hundred in seconds.

learn.discord-raid.s2.h.message: Raid, nuke, or spam: what's the difference?

learn.discord-raid.s2.intro.message: These three terms are often confused, yet they describe very different attacks. And the distinction changes how you protect against them.

learn.discord-raid.s2.raid.what.message: A wave of accounts joins the server to disrupt and spam it through sheer numbers.

learn.discord-raid.s2.nuke.what.message: A member or bot with elevated permissions (a compromised admin, a malicious bot) destroys the server: deleting channels and roles, mass bans.

learn.discord-raid.s2.spam.what.message: A flood of repeated messages, often the visible symptom of a raid, but possible from a single account too.

learn.discord-raid.s2.summary.message: In short: a {raid} is an invasion by numbers, a {nuke} is destruction through permission abuse, and {spam} is the most visible symptom of both.

learn.discord-raid.s3.h.message: What are the consequences for your server?

learn.discord-raid.s3.i1.message: The chat gets drowned out: real conversations become unreadable.

learn.discord-raid.s3.i2.message: Scam links and shocking content are pushed to your members.

learn.discord-raid.s3.i3.message: Members leave the server and your reputation takes a hit.

learn.discord-raid.s3.i4.message: Your moderation team is overwhelmed and burns out.

learn.discord-raid.s4.h.message: How to protect your server from raids?

learn.discord-raid.s4.intro.message: No single measure is enough: solid anti-raid protection relies on several complementary layers.

learn.discord-raid.s4.i1.b.message: A {link} forces every new member to prove they're human, which blocks waves of bots before they reach the server.

learn.discord-raid.s4.i2.b.message: The {link} spots an abnormal spike in connections and locks the server down while the wave passes.

learn.discord-raid.s4.i3.b.message: A {link} channel lures automated accounts and punishes them without ever touching real members.

learn.discord-raid.s4.i4.b.message: Only entrust sensitive roles to trusted people, to also limit the risk of a nuke.

learn.discord-raid.s4.outro.message: This is exactly what RaidProtect automates: the bot protects over {count} today and has already blocked millions of spam messages.

learn.discord-raid.faq.a1.message: Organizing or taking part in a raid to harm a server violates Discord's Terms of Service and can lead to the suspension of the accounts involved. Depending on the content shared, it can also amount to harassment.

learn.discord-raid.faq.q2.message: How many accounts does it take to call it a raid?

learn.discord-raid.faq.a2.message: There's no official threshold. A raid is defined by coordination and simultaneity, not by a precise number: from a few dozen accounts to several thousand via bots.

learn.discord-raid.faq.q3.message: How do you stop a raid that's already underway?

learn.discord-raid.faq.a3.message: Lock down the server (close off arrivals and channels), kick the recently joined accounts, then check permissions. A bot like RaidProtect detects the wave and applies this lockdown automatically.

learn.discord-raid.faq.q4.message: Are a raid and a nuke the same thing?

learn.discord-raid.faq.a4.message: No. A raid comes from the outside (a wave of accounts pouring in), while a nuke comes from the inside (a member or bot with permissions that destroys the server). The two call for different protections.

learn.honeypot-warming.metaTitle.message: "Active" HoneyPot Channel: Do You Need a Bot to Keep It Busy?
learn.honeypot-warming.metaTitle.description: Learn explainer meta title: honeypot activity

learn.honeypot-warming.metaDescription.message: Do you need to run a bot posting messages so a HoneyPot channel looks active? No: here's simply why it's pointless.
learn.honeypot-warming.metaDescription.description: Learn explainer meta description: honeypot activity

learn.honeypot-warming.title.message: Do you need a bot to keep a HoneyPot channel "active"?

learn.honeypot-warming.definition.message: No. A HoneyPot channel doesn't need to be "kept busy" by a bot. To tell whether a channel is active, you have to read the messages... and therefore see who wrote them. Fake activity is instantly spottable, and in any case the accounts that spam don't run that check.

learn.honeypot-warming.s1.h.message: Reminder: what is a HoneyPot channel?

learn.honeypot-warming.s1.p1.message: A {hp} channel is a trap: no real member has any reason to post in it. So any account that posts there is almost certainly a spammer, and it gets punished automatically. It's a simple and formidable way to catch {bot}.

learn.honeypot-warming.s2.h.message: The misconception: "the channel needs to look alive"

learn.honeypot-warming.s2.p1.message: You sometimes read this advice: run a bot that posts messages in the HoneyPot to "warm" it up, so spammers think it's active and come post there. The intention sounds logical... but it doesn't hold up, and it's actually counterproductive.

learn.honeypot-warming.s3.p1.message: Ask yourself: how do you know a channel is "active"? You have to read its latest messages. There's no other way.

learn.honeypot-warming.s3.p2.message: And there's the problem: {strong}. Every message shows its author. So if a bot "warmed up" the channel, anyone looking would see that all the activity comes from one and the same bot. The trick is obvious right away.

learn.honeypot-warming.s3.p3.message: In other words: there's no way to "cleverly" automate a fake living channel. The author of the messages always gives away the fact that the activity is fake.

learn.honeypot-warming.s4.p1.message: There's an even simpler point. To check a channel's activity before sending accounts to it, an attacker would have to log in, pull the message history, and analyze it. That's heavy, costly, and slow.

learn.honeypot-warming.s4.p2.message: But the people who automate accounts to mass-spam don't do that: it's far too complicated and heavy for nothing. They send their accounts everywhere, without asking the question.

learn.honeypot-warming.s4.p3.message: The result: {strong}. It doesn't need to look alive. On the contrary, the less legitimate activity there is, the more any single message becomes a reliable alarm signal.

learn.honeypot-warming.s5.i1.message: Leave your HoneyPot channel empty: don't write in it, and don't put a bot there to keep it busy.

learn.honeypot-warming.s5.i2.message: Fake activity is spottable (the author of each message is visible) and fools no one.

learn.honeypot-warming.s5.i3.message: In any case, automated spammers don't check a channel's activity: it's too costly for them.

learn.honeypot-warming.faq.q1.message: Should I write in my HoneyPot channel?

learn.honeypot-warming.faq.a1.message: No. It should stay empty and silent: no real member has any reason to post there, so any message in it is a reliable signal of an unwanted account.

learn.honeypot-warming.faq.q2.message: Does a bot "warming up" the channel help?

learn.honeypot-warming.faq.a2.message: No. It creates fake activity that's easy to spot, because the author of each message is visible, and it burns resources for nothing.

learn.honeypot-warming.faq.q3.message: Do spammers check whether a channel is active?

learn.honeypot-warming.faq.a3.message: In practice, no. Analyzing a channel's activity before posting would be far too heavy and too costly: automated accounts spam without running that check.

learn.honeypot-warming.faq.q4.message: So how does a HoneyPot trap bots?

learn.honeypot-warming.faq.a4.message: Precisely because it's silent: since no legitimate person writes there, any account that posts gives itself away and can be punished automatically.

learn.least-privilege.metaTitle.message: Least Privilege on Discord: The Best Anti-Nuke Defense
learn.least-privilege.metaTitle.description: Learn article meta title: least privilege

learn.least-privilege.metaDescription.message: Least privilege means giving each member and bot only the permissions they strictly need. Why it's your best anti-nuke defense, and how to apply it.
learn.least-privilege.metaDescription.description: Learn article meta description: least privilege

learn.least-privilege.title.message: The principle of least privilege on Discord

learn.least-privilege.definition.message: The principle of least privilege means giving each member and each bot only the permissions strictly necessary for their role, and nothing more. The fewer all-powerful accounts there are, the less damage a compromised account can do.

learn.least-privilege.s1.p1.message: Each person and each bot only gets {strong}. On Discord, that means avoiding handing out the "Administrator" permission left and right, favoring granular permissions split by role (manage messages, kick, manage channels...), and keeping a clear role hierarchy.

learn.least-privilege.s2.h.message: Why it's your best anti-nuke defense

learn.least-privilege.s2.p1.message: Most {nuke} come from a privileged account: a staff member whose account is compromised (via a {token} or phishing), or a malicious bot with too many permissions. If no one has more permissions than they need, even a hacked account can't destroy everything. Least privilege reduces the blast radius.

learn.least-privilege.s3.i1.message: Only grant "Administrator" to a very small number of trusted people.

learn.least-privilege.s3.i2.message: Favor granular permissions per role rather than global admin.

learn.least-privilege.s3.i3.message: Remove admin from bots that don't need it: a single compromised bot can nuke on its own.

learn.least-privilege.s3.i5.message: Regularly check who has which permissions: RaidProtect's {link} spots risky permissions.

learn.least-privilege.s4.h.message: Going further: locking down access to sensitive roles

learn.least-privilege.s4.p1.message: Least privilege reduces the number of powerful accounts, but those accounts remain a prime target. That's where RaidProtect's Authentication Manager comes in.

learn.least-privilege.s4.p2.message: The {link} protects access to sensitive roles with a real identity check (passkey, PIN, or OTP): getting the role requires authenticating via {auth}. Above all, access is granted for a temporary session that expires, after which the sensitive role is removed automatically.

learn.least-privilege.s4.p3.message: The result: even if a staff member's account is compromised, the attacker doesn't get {strong}. They'd also have to pass the authentication, and the access window stays short. It's least privilege applied not only to "who", but also to "for how long".

learn.least-privilege.faq.q1.message: What is least privilege, in plain terms?

learn.least-privilege.faq.a1.message: Giving each member and each bot just what they need, nothing more. The fewer all-powerful accounts there are, the less damage a compromised account can cause.

learn.least-privilege.faq.q2.message: How does least privilege protect against a nuke?

learn.least-privilege.faq.a2.message: A nuke almost always comes from a privileged account. By limiting everyone's permissions, a compromised account can't delete channels or mass-ban: it simply doesn't have the right to.

learn.least-privilege.faq.q3.message: Should you give a bot administrator?

learn.least-privilege.faq.a3.message: Only if it genuinely needs it. A bot with too many permissions is a risk: favor targeted permissions, and only grant admin to trusted bots that require it.

learn.least-privilege.faq.q4.message: What's the connection with the Authentication Manager?

learn.least-privilege.faq.a4.message: It takes the principle further: it protects access to sensitive roles with an identity check and temporary sessions, so a compromised account doesn't keep permanent administrator access.

learn.self-bot.metaTitle.message: Discord Self-Bot: Definition and Risks for Your Server

learn.self-bot.metaDescription.message: A self-bot automates a Discord user account via the API, which Discord forbids. What it is, how it's used for raids and spam, and how to protect against it.

learn.self-bot.definition.message: A self-bot is a Discord user account (not a real bot) driven automatically by a script that uses the API in its place. It's forbidden by Discord's Terms of Service.

learn.self-bot.s1.h.message: Self-bot or regular bot: what's the difference?

learn.self-bot.s1.p1.message: An official bot is registered with Discord, added through an authorization, displays an "APP" badge, and only has the permissions you grant it. A self-bot, on the other hand, hijacks a normal human account to act on its own.

learn.self-bot.s2.p1.message: Used maliciously, self-bots mainly serve to act en masse while posing as real users:

learn.self-bot.s2.i1.message: Inflating {link}: hundreds of self-bots join a server to spam it simultaneously.

learn.self-bot.s2.i2.message: Sending scams and advertising via direct message at scale.

learn.self-bot.s2.i3.message: Scraping a server's member list to target them elsewhere.

learn.self-bot.s3.p1.message: Automating a user account violates Discord's Terms of Service and risks the account being banned. For a server, the real danger lies elsewhere: a self-bot is hard to tell apart from a normal member, which lets it slip under the radar of standard moderation.

learn.self-bot.s4.h.message: How to protect your server from self-bots?

learn.self-bot.s4.i1.b.message: A {link} stops most self-bot farms before they even reach the server.

learn.server-raidable.metaTitle.message: "This Server Is Raidable": What It Means and How to Fix It
learn.server-raidable.metaTitle.description: Learn explainer meta title: this server is raidable

learn.server-raidable.metaDescription.message: A bot like Jalapeno shows "this server is raidable"? That message only flags that external apps are allowed. What it really means, and how to protect your server.
learn.server-raidable.metaDescription.description: Learn explainer meta description: this server is raidable

learn.server-raidable.title.message: "This server is raidable": should you worry?

learn.server-raidable.definition.message: The "this server is raidable" message comes from a bot like Jalapeno, installed as a user app. It simply flags that your members can use external apps, which could be used to spam via follow-up messages. It's not a flaw in itself, and two settings are enough to protect against it.

learn.server-raidable.s1.h.message: Where does external-app spam come from?

learn.server-raidable.s1.p1.message: Discord lets you install apps directly on your account, the "user apps". Once installed, you can use their commands in any server that allows external apps, even if the app isn't added there.

learn.server-raidable.s1.p2.message: Some malicious apps take advantage of this: through a command, they send a burst of follow-up messages into the channel, which lets them {spam} a server without even being invited. The message appears under the app's name, but it's a member who triggered it.

learn.server-raidable.s2.h.message: "This server is raidable": what it really means

learn.server-raidable.s2.p1.message: Bots like Jalapeno offer a command that displays "this server is raidable". In reality, this test just checks one single thing: do members have permission to use external apps? If so, it shows "raidable".

learn.server-raidable.s2.p2.message: It's misleading. Having that permission enabled doesn't mean your server is defenseless. And above all, watch out for the trap: {strong}, because an administrator bypasses all permissions. You could believe there's a problem that doesn't exist, even after fixing it.

learn.server-raidable.s3.h.message: How to fix "this server is raidable"

learn.server-raidable.s3.intro.message: Two solutions, depending on whether or not you want to keep external apps.

learn.server-raidable.s3.i1.b.message: In the @everyone role permissions (or per channel), remove "Use External Apps". Members will no longer be able to trigger user apps. Be sure to test with a non-administrator account: an admin bypasses the permission and will still see "raidable".

learn.server-raidable.s3.i2.b.message: If you'd rather keep external apps (they have legitimate uses), RaidProtect's {link} detects follow-up message spam, traces it back to the member who triggered it, and punishes them automatically. Those who try to "raid" you this way get kicked out immediately.

learn.server-raidable.faq.q1.message: What does "this server is raidable" mean?

learn.server-raidable.faq.a1.message: That your members can use external apps, which could be used to spam a channel via follow-up messages. It's not a flaw in itself.

learn.server-raidable.faq.a2.message: It just checks one permission. And if you test with an administrator account, it will always show "raidable", because admins bypass permissions. Take it with a lot of skepticism.

learn.server-raidable.faq.q3.message: How do you get rid of the "this server is raidable" message?

learn.server-raidable.faq.a3.message: Disable "Use External Apps" for members (testing with a non-admin account), or add RaidProtect, whose anti-spam spots and punishes these attempts.

learn.server-raidable.faq.q4.message: Do you really need to disable external apps?

learn.server-raidable.faq.a4.message: Not necessarily: they have legitimate uses. With an anti-spam like RaidProtect's, you can keep them while staying protected against follow-up message spam.

learn.spam-discord.metaTitle.message: Discord Spam: What It Is and How to Stop It
learn.spam-discord.metaTitle.description: Learn article meta title: Discord spam

learn.spam-discord.metaDescription.message: Discord spam is the sending of unsolicited, repetitive messages on a server or in DMs. Its forms, why it's a problem, and how to stop it.
learn.spam-discord.metaDescription.description: Learn article meta description: Discord spam

learn.spam-discord.definition.message: Discord spam is the sending of unsolicited, repetitive messages on a server or in a direct message: ads, scam links, fake Nitro, mass mentions. It can come from a single account as well as an entire wave.

learn.spam-discord.s1.h.message: The most common forms of spam

learn.spam-discord.s1.i1.message: Rampant self-promotion: links and invites to other servers, posted on a loop.

learn.spam-discord.s1.i2.message: Scam and phishing links: fake "free Nitro", wallet drainers, fake promotions.

learn.spam-discord.s1.i3.message: Flood: @everyone mentions, emojis, or messages repeated very fast to saturate the chat.

learn.spam-discord.s1.i4.message: Direct message spam: your members receive ads or scams in DMs.

learn.spam-discord.s2.h.message: Spam, flood, raid: where does spam fit?

learn.spam-discord.s2.p1.message: Spam refers to the content (unwanted, repetitive messages). {flood} is one form of it, focused on volume and speed, while a {raid} is an invasion of accounts that often uses spam as a weapon. A single account can spam without there being a raid.

learn.spam-discord.s3.i1.message: The chat gets drowned out and real conversations become unreadable.

learn.spam-discord.s3.i2.message: Scam links reach your members and expose your community.

learn.spam-discord.s3.i3.message: Members get tired and leave, and your moderation burns out.

learn.spam-discord.s4.h.message: How to stop spam on your server?

learn.spam-discord.s4.intro.message: The right approach combines several protections that complement each other.

learn.spam-discord.s4.i1.b.message: The {link} spots repetitive messages, abnormal rates, and mass mentions, then punishes on its own.

learn.spam-discord.s4.i2.b.message: A {link} blocks spam bot farms before they reach the server.

learn.spam-discord.s4.i3.b.message: The {link} stops spammers from contacting your members privately.

learn.spam-discord.s4.outro.message: This is what RaidProtect automates: the bot protects over {count} and has already blocked millions of spam messages.

learn.spam-discord.faq.a1.message: Yes: spam violates Discord's Terms of Service. Servers can punish the culprits, and accounts that spam massively can be banned by Discord.

learn.spam-discord.faq.a2.message: Yes. Unlike a raid, spam doesn't require a wave of accounts: a single account, or a self-bot, is enough to spam.

learn.spam-discord.faq.q3.message: How do you block spam automatically?

learn.spam-discord.faq.a3.message: An anti-spam spots repetitive messages, overly fast sends, and mass mentions, and applies a punishment without any action on your part.

learn.spam-discord.faq.q4.message: Are spam and flood the same thing?

learn.spam-discord.faq.a4.message: Flood is a form of spam focused on volume and speed (saturating a channel). All flood is spam, but not all spam is necessarily flood.

learn.token-grabber.metaTitle.message: Discord Token Grabber: How an Account Gets Stolen
learn.token-grabber.metaTitle.description: Learn article meta title: token grabber

learn.token-grabber.metaDescription.message: A token grabber is malware that steals a Discord account's token to hijack it, without a password. How it works and how to protect yourself.
learn.token-grabber.metaDescription.description: Learn article meta description: token grabber

learn.token-grabber.definition.message: A token grabber is malware designed to steal your Discord token, the key that authenticates your account. With that token, an attacker can control your account without a password.

learn.token-grabber.s1.p1.message: The token is a secret string that proves to Discord that it's really you. Your app stores it locally to keep you logged in. Anyone who gets hold of it can log in as you, without a password and without triggering two-factor authentication.

learn.token-grabber.s2.h.message: How a token grabber steals your account

learn.token-grabber.s2.p1.message: The trap almost always arrives through a file or link you're pushed to open:

learn.token-grabber.s2.i1.message: Fake software, cheats, cracks, or "Discord tools" to download.

learn.token-grabber.s2.i2.message: Fake "free Nitro" offers and phishing links.

learn.token-grabber.s2.p2.message: Once run, the program reads the local files where the token is stored and sends it to the attacker, often within seconds and without the slightest visible sign.

learn.token-grabber.s3.p1.message: With your account, the attacker sends scams to your friends and joins your servers. And if you're an admin or moderator, a stolen token is one of the most common ways to {link} a server from the inside: it's the starting point of many attacks.

learn.token-grabber.s4.h.message: How to protect yourself from a token grabber?

learn.token-grabber.s4.i1.b.message: Cheats, cracks, Discord "tools", and files received from unknown sources are the number-one vector.

learn.token-grabber.s4.i2.b.message: "Free Nitro" and links too good to be true are phishing in the vast majority of cases.

learn.token-grabber.s4.i3.b.message: Change your password immediately: that invalidates the stolen token and logs the attacker out.

learn.token-grabber.s4.i4.b.message: That way, even a compromised staff member's account can't destroy everything.

learn.token-grabber.faq.q1.message: Does a token grabber steal my password?

learn.token-grabber.faq.a1.message: No: it steals the session token, which is enough to access the account without the password. That's exactly what makes it dangerous.

learn.token-grabber.faq.q2.message: Does two-factor authentication protect against a token grabber?

learn.token-grabber.faq.a2.message: Not directly, because a token that's already stolen bypasses the login. But it protects the password change and the reconnection, and changing your password invalidates the stolen token.

learn.token-grabber.faq.q3.message: How do I know if my token has been stolen?

learn.token-grabber.faq.a3.message: Watch for any unknown activity: messages you didn't write, servers joined or left, scam DMs sent in your name. At the slightest doubt, change your password.

learn.token-grabber.faq.q4.message: What's the connection with a nuke?

learn.token-grabber.faq.a4.message: A token stolen from an administrator is one of the most common ways to nuke a server: the attacker acts from a legitimate, privileged account.
